title: Pascal's Wager & The Many-Gods Objection
rootClaim: Believing in God is the strictly rational choice under decision-theoretic expected utility calculations.

branches.text: Infinite Expected Utility: A finite investment in religious devotion yields infinite potential reward (heaven), overriding finite costs regardless of low probability.

children.text: Dominance Principle: If God exists, belief grants infinite gain and disbelief grants infinite loss; if God does not exist, finite losses are negligible.
Inauthenticity Objection: An omniscient God would easily spot self-interested pragmatic calculation rather than genuine spiritual faith.
Pascal's Habituation Response: Pragmatic practice (attending rituals, adopting routines) gradually fosters sincere belief and genuine transformation over time.

branches.text: Decision-theoretic flaws: The Many-Gods objection and infinite probability invalidations collapse the mathematical wager.

children.text: Many-Gods Objection: There are infinitely many conceivable deities with mutually exclusive criteria (e.g. a God that rewards non-believers and punishes traditional wagers).
Live Options Restriction: Wagers should only evaluate culturally live options with historical tradition rather than arbitrary imaginary deities.
Arbitrary Arbitraments: Excluding unrevealed or alien deities from decision matrices is logically unwarranted in pure probability calculations.
Finite Life Sacrifice: If God does not exist, dedicating one's earthly life to religious restriction represents a total loss of the only guaranteed finite existence.
Secular Benefit Reply: Religious communities and spiritual practices often yield immediate psychological and social wellbeing in finite life regardless of afterlife existence.

definitions.description: The weighted average of all possible outcomes for a choice, calculated by multiplying each outcome's value by its probability.
A rule in decision theory stating that if Option A yields at least as good outcomes as Option B in all scenarios and better in one, Option A should be chosen.
The counterargument that Pascal's wager fails because there are endless mutually exclusive theological possibilities, nullifying the calculation.
The philosophical claim that people can directly choose their beliefs at will.
